title: Genetic Association Studies of Suicidal Behavior: A Review of the Past 10 Years, Progress, Limitations, and Future Directions

subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review Framework and Literature Search Strategy
subsections.content:
This review was structured as a systematic evidence synthesis guided by PRISMA principles for transparent study identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and reporting ref [1]. We defined suicidal behavior broadly to include suicide death, suicide attempt, and, where explicitly analyzed as a genetically relevant phenotype, suicidal ideation; however, studies focused only on nonsuicidal self-injury were excluded unless suicidal outcomes were separable. To enhance comparability across studies, we prioritized human genetic association designs and organized evidence by candidate-gene, genome-wide, pharmacogenetic, and family-based approaches.

The literature search combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to suicide phenotypes ("suicide," "suicidal behavior," "suicide attempt," "suicidal ideation," "completed suicide") with genetic terms ("gene," "polymorphism," "variant," "SNP," "genome-wide association," "GWAS," "pharmacogenetic," "family study," "linkage"). Searches were performed primarily in PubMed/MEDLINE and supplemented by reference-list screening of prior reviews and influential primary studies. Because the survey centers on the past decade of molecular association research, study selection was anchored to modern psychiatric-genetic reporting standards while also tracing highly cited antecedent signals in biologically plausible systems such as BDNF and stress-response genes ref [3], ref [4], ref [5].

Eligibility criteria emphasized original peer-reviewed studies in human samples that reported analyzable associations between genetic variation and suicidal outcomes. We extracted information on phenotype definition, ascertainment setting, ancestry, sample size, genotyping platform, covariate adjustment, and correction for multiple testing, given that underpowered samples and phenotype heterogeneity have been persistent limitations in psychiatric genetics ref [6], ref [7]. Geographic context was interpreted with reference to OECD high-income settings when considering differences in sampling infrastructure and registry availability for large-scale genetic studies ref [2], while not restricting inclusion exclusively to those countries.

To reduce bias, we gave preference to studies with clear diagnostic characterization, explicit separation of suicide-related phenotypes, and replication or meta-analytic context. Prior evidence syntheses on genetic studies of suicidal behavior informed backward and forward citation tracking and helped identify recurring loci, inconsistent findings, and methodological pitfalls to be revisited in later subsections ref [8], ref [9], ref [10]. This framework allowed the review to balance historical candidate-gene literature with newer genome-wide and treatment-emergent suicidality studies, while maintaining a consistent standard for evidence appraisal ref [5], ref [11].

subsections.subsection_title: Background Scope: Biological and Familial Foundations of Suicidal Behavior
subsections.content:
The background literature motivating genetic association work on suicidal behavior rests on two complementary observations: suicide and suicide attempts occur disproportionately in the context of major psychiatric illness, and they aggregate within families beyond the transmission of diagnosis alone. Epidemiologic and clinical syntheses have consistently linked suicidal acts to mood disorders, substance use, psychosis, and comorbidity, establishing a high-risk psychopathologic substrate for biological investigation ref [7]. Family studies of adolescent suicide victims and broader reviews of familial transmission further suggest that suicidal behavior itself shows intergenerational clustering, supporting the plausibility of partially distinct inherited liability ref [8], ref [14], ref [12].

Twin and family-genetic studies strengthened this inference by estimating a significant heritable component for suicide death, suicide attempts, and self-harm phenotypes, while also demonstrating important environmental contributions ref [11], ref [13], ref [9]. This evidence framed suicidal behavior as a complex phenotype in which genetic susceptibility interacts with developmental and psychosocial exposures rather than as a simple Mendelian trait ref [12], ref [14]. As a result, early molecular studies were guided toward biologically plausible systems already implicated in stress responsivity, affect regulation, and impulsive aggression.

Among these systems, serotonergic dysfunction received particular attention because neurobiological and prospective clinical studies linked altered serotonin signaling to mood disorders, impulsive traits, and suicidal acts ref [6], ref [15]. Parallel work highlighted dysregulation of the sympathetic nervous system, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, and executive control processes in at-risk individuals, broadening the candidate framework beyond monoamines alone ref [10]. These foundations helped justify candidate-gene investigations of loci such as TPH1, SLC6A4, and BDNF, although findings from early association studies were often inconsistent and phenotype-dependent ref [18], ref [16], ref [17].

subsections.subsection_title: Previous Evidence Syntheses Guiding Study Selection
subsections.content:
Study selection was informed by prior evidence syntheses that had already evaluated the most intensively studied candidate loci for suicidal behavior. In particular, meta-analyses of the serotonergic pathway were used to identify repeatedly investigated variants and to clarify where signals were inconsistent or phenotype-dependent. The TPH A218C polymorphism had been synthesized in a dedicated meta-analysis, while a broader systematic review and meta-analysis of SLC6A4 and TPH emphasized that association estimates varied according to whether suicidal ideation, attempt, or completed suicide was used as the endpoint ref [19], ref [20]. These syntheses therefore guided our prioritization of studies with explicit phenotypic definitions and separable outcome categories.

Earlier pooled analyses also helped determine which loci warranted inclusion despite conflicting primary reports. For catecholaminergic genes, one meta-analysis reported no overall association for COMT Val158Met, whereas another suggested a possible COMT signal but not for HTR1B, illustrating how conclusions depended on study composition and analytic framing ref [21], ref [22]. Similarly, the neurotrophic literature was anchored by a meta-analysis of BDNF, complemented by influential primary studies of BDNF Val66Met in major depression and of NTRK2 variation in depressed suicide attempters ref [23], ref [24], ref [25]. Together, these works highlighted the need to capture both broadly replicated and biologically plausible but still unsettled findings.

Finally, prior syntheses indicated that evidentiary appraisal should not be restricted to conventional case-control studies. Because linkage disequilibrium structure, ancestry, and diagnostic heterogeneity could distort simple pooled estimates, we also retained family-based and adolescent-focused association studies when they addressed canonical candidate genes, such as the 5-HT2A T102C family-based report ref [26]. Thus, previous reviews and meta-analyses served not only as a map of the candidate-gene landscape, but also as a practical framework for selecting loci, phenotypes, and study designs requiring reassessment in the subsequent decade.

For the targeted candidate-gene component, literature identification was organized around biologically informed pathways that dominated pre-GWAS suicidality research, especially serotonergic, dopaminergic, monoaminergic, and stress-response systems. Search terms therefore combined suicidal outcomes (suicide, suicide attempt, suicidal behavior, suicidality) with canonical candidate genes including TPH1, TPH2, SLC6A4/5-HTT, HTR1A, HTR1B, HTR2A, MAOA, COMT, DRD2, CRHR1, and broader polyaminergic loci. Gene selection was anchored in the longstanding serotonin hypothesis of suicidal behavior and in functional work identifying TPH2 as a brain-expressed tryptophan hydroxylase isoform, which expanded the candidate-gene field beyond earlier TPH1-centered studies ref [31].

Eligible studies were primarily case-control or family-informed association analyses evaluating suicidal acts or suicide deaths, either across mixed psychiatric samples or within specific disorders such as major depression, schizophrenia, or alcohol dependence. In practice, this captured repeated investigations of TPH1 and TPH2 ref [27], ref [28], ref [29], ref [30]; serotonin receptor variants in HTR1A, HTR1B, and HTR2A ref [32], ref [33], ref [34], ref [35]; broader serotonergic panels and transporter-expression studies involving SLC6A4/5-HTT ref [36], ref [38]; and non-serotonergic candidates including MAOA, COMT, DRD2, CRHR1, and polyaminergic loci ref [37], ref [39], ref [41], ref [42], ref [45], ref [20]. We also noted studies explicitly modeling gene-environment interplay, particularly for 5-HTTLPR and stress exposure, because such designs were common extensions of candidate-gene reasoning in suicidality research ref [40], ref [44].

Consistent with the broader aims of this review, candidate-gene studies were identified not to assume validity of any individual association, but to map the historical logic of locus selection and the phenotypic heterogeneity of the evidence base. This strategy allowed comparison of studies centered on suicidal behavior per se with those embedding suicidality within depressive, impulsive-aggressive, or treatment-response phenotypes, while preserving attention to functional plausibility and pathway-level continuity across the candidate-gene era ref [33], ref [34], ref [35], ref [36], ref [42], ref [20].

To extend beyond classical candidate-gene studies, we also considered genome-wide, pharmacogenetic, and family-based designs because these approaches address complementary inferential problems. Genome-wide analyses offer broader locus discovery without strong prior biological assumptions, as illustrated by studies of treatment-emergent suicidal ideation during citalopram therapy and related analyses of genetic markers in major depression ref [46], ref [48]. Although early genome-wide efforts were constrained by modest sample sizes and heterogeneous phenotyping, they were important in shifting the field toward hypothesis-free interrogation and in highlighting the need for replication across cohorts.

Pharmacogenetic studies were included when suicidal ideation or behavior was examined in the context of antidepressant exposure, since these designs probe gene-by-treatment effects rather than baseline liability alone ref [46], ref [48]. We also retained targeted studies at the interface of biological plausibility and clinical phenotype, including reports on BDNF Val66Met in suicide attempts among depressed patients, serotonergic pathway polymorphisms in adolescent impulsive-aggression and suicidality, and putative neural conduction genes such as SCN8A and VAMP4 ref [49], ref [51], ref [50]. In our framework, such studies were treated as extensions of the association literature rather than equivalent evidence to adequately powered genome-wide discovery.

Family-based studies were additionally considered because they mitigate population stratification and offer a useful complement to case-control association designs. In particular, the haplotype relative risk framework and related transmission-based methods provided the statistical basis for evaluating overtransmission of risk alleles within families ref [47]. However, family-based investigations of suicidal behavior have remained comparatively sparse, and across all three domains—genome-wide, pharmacogenetic, and family-based—the literature has been limited by small samples, inconsistent definitions of suicidal phenotypes, and variable control for psychiatric comorbidity. These considerations informed a selective but inclusive identification strategy for this subsection.

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of suicidal phenotypes have shifted the field beyond hypothesis-driven candidate genes, but early work was constrained by modest sample sizes, heterogeneous phenotyping, and ascertainment within psychiatric cohorts. Initial studies examined suicide attempts in mood disorders, major depression, or broader psychiatric samples and generally failed to identify robust genome-wide significant loci, while still suggesting a polygenic architecture and partial overlap with affective illness liability ref [52], ref [53], ref [54], ref [57]. Related designs targeting completed suicide or suicidal ideation during antidepressant treatment likewise highlighted the difficulty of locus discovery when outcomes are rare, clinically heterogeneous, and embedded in treatment and diagnostic context ref [55], ref [46].

A central lesson from these studies is that phenotype definition matters. GWAS signals differ depending on whether the outcome is suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, treatment-emergent ideation, or suicide death, and whether analyses are conditioned on major depression, bipolar disorder, or broader psychopathology ref [52], ref [54], ref [56], ref [46]. Cross-trait analyses further indicate that suicide attempts share common variant liability with major psychiatric disorders, yet are not fully reducible to them, supporting the view that suicidality-related traits possess both transdiagnostic and phenotype-specific genetic components ref [56].

Overall, GWAS of suicidal phenotypes have been most valuable in clarifying methodology and architecture rather than delivering definitive loci. The literature consistently points to the need for much larger harmonized samples, careful separation of ideation from action, incorporation of ancestry diversity, and meta-analytic frameworks that model comorbidity and environmental exposure. These developments are essential if GWAS is to move from underpowered discovery efforts toward reproducible biological insight and clinically informative risk stratification ref [53], ref [56], ref [57].

Beyond single-locus discovery, polygenic methods have become central for modeling the highly diffuse genetic architecture expected for suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Polygenic risk scores (PRS) aggregate effects across many variants and can quantify shared liability with major depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, impulsivity, and related traits, but their performance depends strongly on discovery-sample size, trait heritability, linkage disequilibrium (LD) structure, and ancestry matching between discovery and target samples ref [58], ref [60], ref [62]. In suicidality research, these constraints are especially salient because phenotypic heterogeneity and low base rates attenuate signal and reduce out-of-sample prediction.

The statistical framework used to generate and evaluate PRS is therefore consequential. Early pruning-and-thresholding approaches remain common, but newer shrinkage and Bayesian methods that better account for LD and infinitesimal architectures generally improve prediction for complex psychiatric traits ref [58], ref [62]. At the discovery stage, appropriate control of multiple testing remains essential; empirically derived estimates of the effective number of independent tests help refine genome-wide significance thresholds across genotyping and imputation platforms ref [59]. For suicidal phenotypes, where case definitions range from ideation to attempts and death, harmonization, misclassification control, and cross-cohort comparability are as important as analytic sophistication.

Family-based and genetically informed designs add another layer of complexity. Suicidality often clusters within families through both inherited liability and shared environmental adversity, making standard GWAS assumptions vulnerable to confounding by relatedness, ascertainment, and non-independence ref [61]. Mixed models, transmission-based tests, within-family PRS analyses, and methods that partition direct genetic effects from familial or environmental background can strengthen causal interpretation. More broadly, contemporary complex-trait toolkits integrate PRS with SNP-heritability, genetic correlation, fine-mapping, pathway analysis, and functional annotation, providing a more coherent framework for moving from association signals toward biologically and clinically interpretable models of suicide risk ref [58].

Structural genomic variation, particularly copy number variants (CNVs), has been investigated far less extensively than common SNP-based risk in suicidal behavior, but it remains a plausible source of liability because rare deletions or duplications can exert relatively large effects on neurodevelopmental and synaptic pathways. Early genome-wide CNV studies of suicidal phenotypes were therefore motivated by the possibility that rare, high-impact variation might help explain risk not captured by GWAS of common alleles ref [63], ref [64].

The available evidence, however, has been modest and heterogeneous. A genome-wide CNV study of suicidal behavior reported no single recurrent CNV of large effect that clearly distinguished cases from controls, underscoring the difficulty of detecting robust signals in small samples and clinically heterogeneous phenotypes ref [63]. Similarly, in major depressive disorder, CNV analyses comparing suicide attempters with non-attempters did not identify definitive, replicable loci, although they suggested that CNV burden or disruption of neurobiologically relevant genes could warrant further study ref [64]. These findings are broadly consistent with the wider psychiatric genetics literature, where rare structural variants often show stronger relationships with severe neurodevelopmental disorders than with narrowly defined suicidal outcomes.

Overall, CNV research in suicidology is constrained by limited sample size, inconsistent phenotype definition, variable laboratory and calling pipelines, and the rarity of individual events. Future progress will likely depend on very large harmonized cohorts, sequencing-informed detection of structural variants beyond array-based CNVs, and integrative analyses that test whether rare genomic rearrangements converge with polygenic risk, transcriptomic dysregulation, and environmental adversity in shaping suicidal behavior ref [63], ref [64].

Epigenomic studies have sought molecular mechanisms that might connect environmental adversity to altered gene regulation in suicide. Early postmortem work reported promoter-wide hypermethylation of ribosomal RNA genes in suicide brains, suggesting dysregulation of nucleolar function and cellular stress responses rather than changes confined to classic neurotransmitter loci ref [65]. Other candidate epigenetic studies implicated polyamine-system genes: altered methylation and expression of spermine synthase and spermine oxidase in suicide completers supported a model in which stress-responsive metabolic pathways contribute to risk through transcriptional remodeling ref [66].

Neurotrophin signaling has been another recurrent theme. Increased methylation at BDNF promoters in cortical tissue from suicide subjects was associated with reduced expression, consistent with broader evidence linking impaired synaptic plasticity and stress adaptation to suicidal phenotypes ref [67]. Among the more replicated blood-based findings, variation in methylation at SKA2—considered alongside underlying genotype—was reported to predict suicidal behavior and PTSD-related stress vulnerability, highlighting the importance of integrating sequence and epigenetic information in the same analytic framework ref [68].

Overall, epigenomic evidence remains suggestive rather than definitive. Most studies are modest in size, rely on heterogeneous tissues, and are vulnerable to confounding by diagnosis, medication exposure, substance use, smoking, trauma history, and postmortem factors. In addition, tissue- and cell-type specificity complicates inference from peripheral biomarkers to brain mechanisms. Future progress will likely depend on larger epigenome-wide designs, joint modeling of genotype, methylation, and expression, and longitudinal sampling to distinguish state-related signatures from stable liability markers relevant to suicidal behavior ref [65], ref [66], ref [67], ref [68].

Before the GWAS era, molecular studies of suicidal behavior were dominated by candidate-gene designs motivated by serotonergic, dopaminergic, neurotrophic, and stress-response hypotheses. Meta-analytic evidence from this literature is mixed: modest associations have been reported for BDNF ref [23], the TPH A218C variant ref [19], and COMT, whereas evidence for HTR1B has generally been negative ref [22]. For SLC6A4 and TPH, pooled effects appear highly sensitive to phenotype definition, with differences emerging across suicide attempt, medically serious attempt, and broader suicidality constructs ref [20]. These inconsistencies illustrate a core limitation of candidate-gene work: biological plausibility rarely compensated for small samples, heterogeneous ascertainment, and incomplete correction for multiple testing.

Candidate-gene studies also highlighted the importance of intermediate clinical dimensions. In adolescents, polymorphisms across serotonergic pathway genes were examined not only against suicidal acts, but also against impulsive-aggression and related traits that may index liability more proximally than the binary outcome itself ref [51]. Similarly, stress-system candidates have been evaluated in diagnostic subgroups, with HPA-axis variation showing possible relevance to suicidal behavior in schizophrenia ref [45]. Such findings were useful in framing mechanistic hypotheses, but most effects have proven difficult to replicate consistently across cohorts, ancestries, and clinical settings ref [20], ref [22].

Familial studies provided a broader genetic context and remain important because they predated molecular discovery while offering robust evidence that suicidal behavior aggregates within families beyond transmission of major psychiatric disorders alone ref [8], ref [14]. Controlled family studies of adolescent suicide victims, alongside wider reviews of family-genetic designs, support partial familial specificity for suicidal behavior, although shared environment, assortative mating, and comorbid psychopathology complicate causal interpretation ref [8], ref [14]. Taken together, the candidate-gene and family literatures helped establish heritable liability, but their principal contemporary value is heuristic: they identify phenotypic heterogeneity, familial aggregation, and plausible biological systems that are now better tested using genome-wide and integrative approaches.

Over the past decade, the field has moved from small candidate-gene reports toward large-scale, collaborative psychiatric genetics. This shift is visible in the growth of consortia-based analyses, standardized imputation and quality-control pipelines, and explicit attention to reproducibility and sharing across cohorts ref [69], ref [70], ref [71]. Administrative infrastructure has therefore become inseparable from scientific progress: biobank-enabled ascertainment, harmonized phenotyping, and cross-site governance now largely determine whether suicidal thoughts, attempts, and deaths can be studied with adequate statistical power ref [72], ref [73], ref [74].

A central scholarly issue is phenotype definition. Studies variably analyze suicide attempt, suicide death, self-harm, or broad suicidality composites, often using electronic health records, structured interviews, or registry linkages, each with different misclassification profiles ref [75], ref [76], ref [77]. This heterogeneity complicates comparison across studies and can attenuate SNP-based signals, even as recent GWAS have demonstrated that meaningful common-variant associations are detectable for suicide attempt and related phenotypes when sample sizes are sufficiently large ref [78], ref [79], ref [80].

Administrative and ethical constraints remain especially salient because suicide-related data are sensitive and frequently collected in clinical, military, or mortality-surveillance settings. Best practice increasingly requires transparent preregistration where possible, rigorous control for ancestry and sample overlap, careful treatment of comorbidity, and governance frameworks that enable secure data sharing without compromising privacy ref [81], ref [82], ref [83]. Future reviews should therefore document not only findings, but also cohort provenance, consent and linkage procedures, phenotype harmonization rules, and analytic reporting standards, as these scholarly and administrative features materially shape inference in genetic studies of suicidal behavior ref [70], ref [74], ref [84].
